paragraphs: §1 — The summary scope of the refutation; the abrogation-claim is self-contradictory because Muḥammad himself affirmed the Torah

What we set down here of the refutation of them is a small portion, in keeping with what the place can bear, since we have already composed on that subject a separate book. We have said in what preceded that every report whose reporter calls, in it, to that which reason rules impossible and corrupts, has no need [for inquiry] into its source, nor into those from whom it was transmitted — whether they are such as collusion (al-tawāṭuʾ) and lying are admissible of, or not. And by this very discourse the report of Muḥammad is invalidated, since he called to that which reason rules impossible, together with self-contradiction (al-munāqaḍa) also in what he called to. That is, he affirmed the prophethood of Moses (peace be upon him), and gave credence to those who transmitted his miracles, and verified the Torah and all that is in it, and called its people, and those in whose hands it is, to bear witness — in more than one place of his book — [as] he relates of his Lord, who said to him [קראן 5:43] "wa-kayfa yuḥakkimūnaka wa-ʿindahum al-Tawrātu fīhā ḥukmu llāhi" ("and how do they make you a judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God?"); and of that also is his saying [שם 10:94] "fa-in kunta fī shakkin mimmā anzalnā ilayka fa-sʾal alladhīna yaqraʾūna l-kitāba min qablika" ("and if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down to you, then ask those who read the Scripture before you"); and he says also [שם 16:43] "fa-sʾalū ahla l-dhikri" ("then ask the people of the remembrance"). So he, in more than one place of his book, verifies the Torah and calls its people, and those in whose hands it is, to bear witness — and it is absurd that one should call to bear witness one who is, in his view, a liar.

: al-kitāb al-mufrad — Q here, and again at the close of the bab (§16) and in Bab 16 §4, refers to a separate, dedicated anti-Muslim work he composed ("the book I composed against them," al-kitāb alladhī allaftuhu ʿalayhim / jarradnāhu ʿalayhim), in which, he says, he treated the matter "bab by bab" and recorded debates he had had with Muslim mutakallimūn. This work is not extant; the present bab is his condensed treatment "in keeping with what the place can bear" (mā yaḥtamiluhu al-mawḍiʿ). The phrase recurs as a deferral formula throughout the bab. : The opening move is the tu quoque-by-self-contradiction that governs the whole first third of the bab. Q's strategy: the Qurʾān itself repeatedly affirms the authority of the Torah and appeals to "those who read the Scripture before you" (Q 5:43, 10:94, 16:43) — so Muḥammad cannot consistently both vouch for the Torah and claim it was abrogated or that it foretold him without containing what it in fact lacks. Note that Q quotes the Qurʾān in Arabic (rendered here in transliteration) with Hebrew-script pointers to sūra and verse; the OCR of these pointers was heavily corrupted (diff-report p207 rows 5–10) and is reconstructed from the standard references (Q 5:43, 10:94, 16:43). al-munāqaḍa (self-contradiction) and al-tawāṭuʾ (collusion in transmission) are the two pillars of the argument.
§2 — Scripture and transmission both affirm the perpetuity of the Torah: the Sabbath and the festivals are "an everlasting statute"

[Muḥammad in more than one place of his book verifies the Torah and calls its people to bear witness, and those in whose hands it is;] and it is absurd that one should call to bear witness one who is, in his view, a liar. Then we refute that [further] by [noting] that he alleged that the law of the Torah has [already] been abrogated (nusikhat), and that something else has been substituted for it — [something else] than that of which the one who brought it informed that it is not abrogated and does not lapse, and that it is binding until the passing-away of the world. And that [perpetuity] is [established] in the text (al-naṣṣ) and in the transmission (al-naql). As for the text: it is the saying of Moses (peace be upon him) [Num 15:23] אֵת כָּל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יי אֲלֵיכֶם בְּיַד מֹשֶׁה מִן הַיּוֹם אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יי וָהָלְאָה לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם. For his saying וָהָלְאָה [means] "and thenceforward (halumma jarran), without interruption and without end, until the world passes away." And his saying concerning the Sabbath [Exod 31:16] וְשָׁמְרוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת הַשַּׁבָּת לְדֹרֹתָם בְּרִית עוֹלָם — so he informed that the Sabbath, and the keeping of it, and the resting on it, is binding for all time. And likewise he said concerning the Feast of Weeks (ḥag Shavuʿot) [Lev 23:21] חֻקַּת עוֹלָם בְּכָל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם — so he brought in that three things that indicate perpetuation (al-taʾyīd): the first, his saying עוֹלָם ("everlasting"); the second, his saying "in all your dwellings" (בְּכָל מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם); and the third, his saying לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם ("throughout your generations"). And this is at the utmost of emphasis.

: The "text" (naṣṣ) leg of the perpetuity argument. Q stacks three pentateuchal formulae — Num 15:23 (wa-halʾah le-dorotekhem), Exod 31:16 (the Sabbath as berit ʿolam), Lev 23:21 (the Feast of Weeks as ḥuqqat ʿolam) — and parses the triple intensifier of Lev 23:21 (ʿolam + be-khol moshvotekhem + le-dorotekhem) as a deliberate piling-up of perpetuity markers. The argument anticipates and forecloses the Islamic doctrine of naskh (abrogation): a divinely promulgated law explicitly stamped "everlasting … in all your dwellings … throughout your generations" cannot be abrogated by a later revelation. The OCR scrambled these citations and their pointers badly (diff-report p206 rows 0–13); the merged multimodal text restores them, and the references (Num 15:23, Exod 31:16, Lev 23:21) follow Q's marginal pointers.
§3 — Malachi seals the prophets with a command to keep the Torah; Daniel forecloses any later prophet

And again: Malachi (peace be upon him), who is the seal of the prophets — for he is the last-mentioned of the prophets — says, in his mention of the Day of Judgment [Mal 3:22] זִכְרוּ תּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה עַבְדִּי אֲשֶׁר צִוִּיתִי אוֹתוֹ בְחֹרֵב עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל חֻקִּים וּמִשְׁפָּטִים, and says right after that [Mal 3:23] הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי שֹׁלֵחַ לָכֶם אֵת אֵלִיָּה הַנָּבִיא לִפְנֵי בּוֹא יוֹם יי הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא. So he commanded the keeping of the Torah — which is its keeping and the upholding of its ordinances — until that day, which is the Day of Judgment; and neither he nor any other of the prophets mentioned that God (great and mighty) would legislate a [new] law, or would command the imposition of anything other than the Torah and its ordinances.

And again: we found Daniel (peace be upon him) informed that prophecy is sealed and that God will not raise up a [further] prophet — that being in his saying [Dan 9:24] לַחְתֹּם חָזוֹן וְנָבִיא, and he says [in the alternative reading, Dan 9:24] וּלְהָתֵם חָזוֹן וְנָבִיא.

: That Malachi is "the seal of the prophets" (khātim al-nabiyyīn) "because he is the last-mentioned of the prophets" is a pointed appropriation: khātam al-nabiyyīn is the Qurʾān's own title for Muḥammad (Q 33:40). Q turns it against the Muslims — the true seal is Malachi, the last of the canonical prophets, whose parting command is precisely to keep the Torah (Mal 3:22) until the eschaton, and whose final foretelling is of Elijah (Mal 3:23), not of a new lawgiver. : Q gives two readings of Dan 9:24: the Masoretic la-ḥtom ("to seal up vision and prophet," from ḥ-t-m) and the variant u-le-hatem ("to bring to an end / complete," from t-m-m) — both serving his point that vision and prophecy are concluded with the seventy weeks. He returns to Dan 9:24-26 at length in Bab 6 §13 (the "anointed one cut off"). On either reading, Q's inference is that no prophet comes after the sealing — foreclosing Muḥammad's claim a priori.
§4 — The "sealing applied only to Israel" evasion: the prophecy was general and admits no exception without proof
So Daniel informed that revelation (al-waḥy) and prophecy are sealed, so that after the seventy weeks (al-sabʿīn al-asābīʿ) which he mentioned and detailed there is neither revelation nor prophet.

Then some of them [the Muslims] alleged concerning that, that he sealed prophecy only from the house of Israel, and informed that God will not make a prophet of any one of them nor send from them a messenger — but as for others, it is admissible that a prophet should come from among them. To them it is said: as for the statement [in Daniel], it came only as a general statement, and it singled out no one to the exclusion of another; so it is not admissible for them to say that and to affirm it save by a standing proof (burhān qāʾim). And if they claim that the proof which made it [necessarily] specified is the establishment of the prophethood of their man (ṣāḥibihim) and what stood for him of the proofs and the miracles (al-barāhīn wa-l-muʿjizāt) — those which it is inadmissible that any bring their like save a sent prophet — then we shall speak on that hereafter.

: Q anticipates the standard Muslim rejoinder: Daniel sealed prophecy only among Israelites, leaving room for a gentile prophet (Muḥammad as an Ishmaelite). Q's reply is methodological: the Danielic sealing-statement is general (ʿumūman) and singles out no group; to restrict it to Israel requires an independent burhān. The only candidate proof would be Muḥammad's own established prophethood — which is precisely what is in dispute (a petitio) — and whose alleged supports (the barāhīn of the Qurʾān's iʿjāz and the reported muʿjizāt) Q promises to dismantle in §§11–16. ṣāḥibuhum ("their man / their master") is Q's standing oblique designation for Muḥammad throughout the bab.
§5 — God would not abrogate Moses' law through a universal prophet without forewarning by Moses; the dispersion-and-ingathering promises concern the Messiah, not Muḥammad

Then it is said to them: how is it admissible that God (great and mighty) should have known that He wished to abrogate the law of Moses (peace be upon him) and his Torah at the hand of a prophet whom He sends to all the people of the earth — the white and the black — commanding the whole of them to adopt a [new] law, and yet should not give notice of that at the hand of the chief of the sent ones, Moses (peace be upon him), nor at the hand of any other of the rest of the prophets (upon them be mercy) — and this together with the fact that Moses and others of the prophets did inform of what He wills to come to pass until the utmost of the ages and epochs?

Of that is the saying of the chief of mankind, Moses (peace be upon him), and his informing of the exile of the nation and its scattering to the far reaches of the earth, then what will come of its gathering and return — for he says [Deut 28:64] וֶהֱפִיצְךָ יְיָ בְּכָל הָעַמִּים מִקְצֵה הָאָרֶץ וְעַד קְצֵה הָאָרֶץ, then he says [Deut 30:4] אִם יִהְיֶה נִדַּחֲךָ בִּקְצֵה הַשָּׁמַיִם מִשָּׁם יְקַבֶּצְךָ יְיָ אֱלֹהֶיךָ וּמִשָּׁם יִקָּחֶךָ, and what he mentioned after that of the return of the good things and their multiplication. And these are the promises which the rest of the prophets expounded and gave good tidings of — of the coming of the Messiah, and what will be in his days.

: The argument from prophetic forewarning: if God meant to abrogate Mosaic law through a universal prophet, the supreme economy of revelation (the most consequential event imaginable) would surely have been announced in advance by Moses or some prophet — yet what they announce for the end-time is the ingathering (Deut 28:64 dispersion; Deut 30:4 regathering) and the Messiah, not a new lawgiver. "The white and the black" (al-abyaḍ wa-l-aswad) is an idiom for "all mankind without distinction," reflecting Islam's claim to universal mission. The transition from the OCR-corrupt pointers (diff-report p205 rows 0–7) to the messianic material is preserved in the merged text.
§6 — The Messiah's age of universal peace; the foretold one should have been the most-announced of all, not unmentioned

[There will be in his days] of the encompassing of safety, the abolition of wars, the vanishing of unbelief, and the becoming of [all] creation upon a single religion and a single tongue — together with what Daniel mentioned of the kingdoms, kingdom after kingdom, down to the coming of the Messiah and his dominion over the kingship of the world. [Given all this,] it ought not to have been that there be added to these sayings and these reports the report of this man and his prophethood and his law; rather, it ought to have been that his report be advanced before every [other] report, and that the mention of him and the good tidings of him be more fitting than the mention of every [other] matter — especially together with what you describe him as, of the magnitude of his rank and the eminence of his measure in heaven and on earth, and that he is the beloved of the Lord of the worlds, and that but for him God would not have created the world. So one who is of this description — it must be that not one of the prophets diverge from mentioning him, so that not one of them mention him at all; rather it ought to have been that the mention of him and the good tidings of him be from the time of Adam onward, at the hand of one and another of them down to the last of them.

: The argumentum e silentio, pressed to its sharpest: on the Muslims' own extravagant Christology-of-Muḥammad — that he is ḥabīb rabb al-ʿālamīn ("the beloved of the Lord of the worlds") and that "but for him God would not have created the world" (lawlāhu mā khalaqa llāhu l-ʿālam, the well-known ḥadīth qudsī lawlāka lawlāka) — the more exalted they make him, the more glaring the prophets' total silence becomes. A figure of cosmic centrality should have been the single most-foretold person in all Scripture, announced "from Adam onward"; he is in fact unmentioned. Q quotes the Muslim superlatives precisely in order to turn them into the premise of a reductio.
§7 — The claim that the prophets did announce him entails the impossibility of any true report at all; the burnt-Torah and Bukhtnaṣṣar evasion

So if they say — and it is [indeed] their statement — that the prophets did give good tidings of him, and that the Torah did mention him, and that the Qurʾān spoke of that: this too is of what proves his lie and the corruption of his claim, since he claimed, against the Torah and the books of the prophets, what is not in them of mention of him. Were there nothing against them but this, there would be in it sufficiency, dispensing with anything else.

And if they say: "Then you are liars in your saying that he is not in the Torah!" — this is the statement of the common folk among them. As for the people of knowledge and inquiry (ahl al-ʿilm wa-l-naẓar), they do not say that, because it follows from it that the Jews — who are a creation beyond numbering for multitude, from East to West — could be guilty of lying, and that what is recorded in their possession, which they recite for all time, could be admissible [as false]: that they hand down this lie and this denial, age after age, throughout the [whole succession of] passing epochs. From this it would follow that there is in the world no sound report at all; and in that is the invalidation of all the prophets, together with the abolition of [their] burden [of authority] (al-ḥaml) also.

So the answer of the people of inquiry among them, concerning that, is along two lines. Some of them allege that the Torah which is in your hands is not the Torah which Moses brought, because that one Bukhtnaṣṣar (Nebuchadnezzar) burnt, and this present one was composed only after that. So these [too] are bound by what bound those others — namely, that the Jews, in their entirety, from East to West,

: The dilemma: either the Torah does foretell Muḥammad (then the Jews who deny it are lying en masse, which Q will show is impossible — and which would dissolve the very possibility of reliable transmission, naql, on which Islam's own claims rest), or it does not (then Muḥammad falsely ascribed to it what it lacks). Q then introduces the first of two Muslim evasions of the first horn: the claim that the present Torah is a post-exilic reconstruction, the original having been burnt by Nebuchadnezzar (Bukhtnaṣṣar) — so the foretelling was lost. al-ḥaml here is the burden/authority of prophetic transmission. ahl al-ʿilm wa-l-naẓar (the learned, the mutakallimūn) are distinguished from al-ʿawāmm (the common folk); the more sophisticated Muslims, knowing the mass-transmission (tawātur) argument cuts against them, do not crudely call the Jews liars.
§8 — The burnt-Torah evasion refuted by mass-transmission; the symbolic-allusion (ramz) evasion and why a universal prophet would never be hidden in allusion

[the Jews, in their entirety, from East to West,] together with the community of the Christians also, report that this Torah which is in their hands is the Torah which Moses (peace be upon him) brought, handing it down from his days to this end-point, with no disagreement among them in that. So if lying were admissible of them in this matter, there would be no sound report upon the earth. Moreover, this statement of theirs is also self-contradictory with what we have already mentioned of the saying of their book and its verifying of the Torah, and its calling the Torah and its people to bear witness, and its saying in more than one place "O People of the Book" (yā ahl al-kitāb). And we shall also mention their argument for this statement, and its corruption, in our invalidating of what they claim of the prophethood of Jesus son of Mary.

And the other party allege that Muḥammad is mentioned in the Torah by way of symbol and allusion (al-ramz wa-l-talwīḥ), [such] that one climbs to the knowledge of that by interpretation and extraction (al-taʾwīl wa-l-istikhrāj), and that the Jews distort that statement and interpret it otherwise than its meaning. This too is like the first, and there binds them in it what bound the others. Furthermore, it is said to them also: in a matter of this magnitude and eminence, and [concerning] this exalted lord whose obedience is obligatory upon all creation and whose law is binding upon them too, the Arab and the non-Arab — why should it have been wished that he be mentioned [only] by symbol and allusion, so that one arrives at the knowledge of that [only] by interpretation and far-fetched extraction, in which much disagreement falls? Rather, it ought to have been that this be made explicit with an explicitness in which no disagreement falls, and that his name be proclaimed with a proclamation that removes doubt and ambiguity from it — just as God (great and mighty), when He wished to give Abraham the good tidings of his son Isaac, informed him of that by plain declaration and explicit naming, without circumlocution; and likewise in His informing David of what He wished to come to pass of his son Solomon; and like the saying of the prophet [1 Kgs 13:2] הִנֵּה בֵן נוֹלָד לְבֵית דָּוִד יֹאשִׁיָּהוּ שְׁמוֹ וג׳; and like the saying of Zechariah (peace be upon him) concerning the Messiah [Zech 6:12] הִנֵּה אִישׁ צֶמַח שְׁמוֹ וּמִתַּחְתָּיו יִצְמָח וג׳. So your man — why was his being mentioned plainly left aside, so that one came to need, for it, the feeble, frail extraction from which nothing is obtained? And we shall mention, in the twenty-fourth bab of this Maqala, of the promises

: The reply to the burnt-Torah evasion is tawātur (mass-transmission): both Jews and Christians, across the whole inhabited world, transmit the present Torah as Moses' Torah without dissent; if such concurrent, geographically dispersed transmission can be false, no report whatever is reliable — which destroys Islam's own epistemic foundation. Q also notes the internal contradiction with the Qurʾān's repeated "O People of the Book" (yā ahl al-kitāb). He defers the fuller treatment to his refutation of the prophethood of Jesus — i.e., the following Bab 16. : The second evasion: Muḥammad is in the Torah cryptically (ramz wa-talwīḥ), recoverable only by taʾwīl and istikhrāj (allegorical interpretation and extraction). Q's reply trades on the disproportion between the alleged universal, binding significance of the prophet and the obscurity of a merely allusive announcement: God announces lesser matters by name — Isaac to Abraham (Gen 17/18), Josiah by name three centuries early (1 Kgs 13:2), the messianic Ṣemaḥ ("Branch") through Zechariah (Zech 6:12). A universal lawgiver would be announced with afṣaḥ, unmistakable explicitness, not buried in allusion subject to "much disagreement." The cross-reference is to Bab 24 of this Maqala on the messianic promises. The Hebrew citations were OCR-corrupt (diff-report p203 rows 0–6) and are restored from the merged text.
§9 — Israel's exile was punishment for forsaking the Torah; restoration comes through return to it — the opposite of abrogation

[We shall mention, in the twenty-fourth bab of this Maqala, of] the promises and good tidings of which the prophets informed that they would be in the days of the Messiah and at the gathering of the house of Israel from the regions of the world and the far reaches of the earth — that which invalidates the statement of the Muslims and the statement of everyone who lays claim to a religion other than the religion of the Torah, of those who affirm a prophethood.

And it is said to them: the exile of the Children of Israel from their land, and the removal of their blessings, their kingship, and their dominion — its cause was only their forsaking of what God commanded them of the ordinances of the Torah, and their contravening of that. And God (mighty and exalted) informed them, at the hands of the company of the prophets (peace be upon them), that the return of their dominion and their kingship, the coming of the Messiah, and the building of the House which Ezekiel (יחזקאל) saw, come about only by [their] returning and repenting; and returning and repenting can only be from something which a person had forsaken and disobeyed in, so that he repents and returns to what was obligatory upon him, and does it and upholds it. And this is the contrary of your statement that that law has [already] been abrogated and nullified, and that the adoption of another in its place has become obligatory.

: A theological argument from the logic of repentance: the prophets condition Israel's restoration (the Messiah, the rebuilt Temple of Ezekiel's vision) on teshuvah — return to the Torah they had abandoned. But "return" presupposes that the thing returned to is still binding; one cannot "return" to an abrogated law. So the very mechanism of restoration the prophets describe refutes the abrogation thesis. This recasts the whole exile-and-return schema as an argument for the Torah's perpetuity. al-Bayt = the (Second/future) Temple; the Ezekiel reference is to the visionary temple of Ezek 40–48, on which Q dwells in Bab 6 §§14–18.

§10 — Whatever bound the Christians binds the Muslims; the nations will keep the Sabbath and the festivals at the redemption; the transmission of the law's perpetuity is as sound as the transmission of the law itself

And there binds them all of what we bound the Christians by, of what the Book mentioned of the coming of the Messiah, and what Ezekiel (יחזקאל) mentioned of the building of the House, and the nations' adopting of the Sabbath, the new moons, the pilgrimage of Tabernacles (ḥag al-maẓāll), and their adopting of the priests (הכהנים) — when Isaiah (ישעיהו) says [Isa 66:23] וּמִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ וּמִדֵּי שַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ וְיָבֹא כָל בָּשָׂר לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֹת לְפָנָי אָמַר יי — so he informed that all flesh adopt the Sabbath at that time; and likewise what Zechariah (peace be upon him) mentioned in his saying [Zech 14:16] וְהָיָה אֲשֶׁר יְגֹף יי אֶת הָעַמִּים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעֲלוּ לָחֹג אֶת חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת, and other than that of his saying and the sayings of others.

And the like of what we bound them by concerning the Jews' transmission of the Torah and the report of Moses — the like of that binds them concerning their [the Jews'] transmission of its perpetuation (taʾbīd). For everyone who transmitted the report of Moses and the reports of his miracles, and [transmitted] that this Torah is the Torah which he brought from God (exalted be He) — they, in their entirety, transmitted that it is inadmissible that it be abrogated or altered, and that it is binding for all time. So if they are veracious in their transmission of the report of Moses and the report of his Torah, then likewise they are veracious in their reporting that his law is not abrogated,

: Two strands. First, the parity-with-the-Christians point: the same eschatological prophecies Q used against the Christians (Bab 6 §§10–18) bind the Muslims equally — Isa 66:23 (all flesh keeping new-moon and Sabbath) and Zech 14:16 (the nations keeping Sukkot) foretell the nations themselves observing the Torah's cult and calendar at the redemption, which is incompatible with the law's abrogation. Second, and decisive, the transmission-parity point completed in §11: the identical chain of naql that conveys "Moses brought this Torah" also conveys "this Torah is never abrogated" — you cannot accept the one transmission and reject the other without arbitrariness. ḥag al-maẓāll = Sukkot (the Feast of Tabernacles/Booths).
§11 — One cannot accept the transmission of the Torah and reject the transmission of its non-abrogation; the two arguments for Muḥammad's prophethood: the Qurʾān's iʿjāz, and the reported miracles

[then likewise they are veracious in their reporting that his law] is not abrogated, and that they took that from him and from the rest of the prophets. And if lying and interpolation (al-tazyīd) are admissible of them concerning [the claim] that it is not abrogated, then the like of that is admissible of them concerning the root (al-aṣl), which is the report of Moses [itself]; and if that is admissible, then there follows what we said — that there is upon the earth no sound report — since every [other] report is below their report in soundness.

We now return to their affirming of his prophethood, and we say: they, in affirming his prophethood and the proof of that, are upon two statements. Some of them allege that his proof of that, and his miracle (muʿjizatuhu), is the Qurʾān which he brought — for there were unable to oppose it (ʿajaza ʿan muʿāraḍatihi) all the people of the [Arabic] language among the Arabs, whose craft was eloquence and fluency (al-balāgha wa-l-faṣāḥa); and that he challenged them with it (taḥaddāhum bihi) and called them to opposition, and made their inability for that a proof. So no one of them succeeded in that — and this was the proof of the soundness of what he claimed of prophethood. And this is what is made explicit in the Qurʾān in more than one place; and there is not mentioned in it that he has any miracle (muʿjiza) or sign (āya) other than it. As for others among them, they — together with their saying that the Qurʾān is his miracle — added to that other miracles which they alleged he performed: such as that he summoned a tree, and it came to him approaching, then he commanded it to return, and it returned to its place; and that he gave drink to a great multitude from scant water; and that there was set before him a poisoned ewe, and the ewe spoke and informed him that it was poisoned, lest he eat of it and perish; and other than that, of what they ascribed to him.

: The hinge from the abrogation-polemic (§§2–10) to the prophethood-proof polemic (§§11–16). Q closes the transmission argument (the naql of non-abrogation is as authoritative as the naql of the Torah itself; rejecting the one impugns the other and so collapses all khabar) and then frames the two Muslim grounds for Muḥammad's prophethood: (a) the iʿjāz al-Qurʾān — the inimitability of the Qurʾān, evidenced by the Arabs' inability (ʿajz) to meet the taḥaddī (challenge) to produce its like (Q 2:23, 17:88, etc.); and (b) supplementary muʿjizāt (the moving tree, watering a multitude from little water, the poisoned ewe that spoke at Khaybar). Q's report that the Qurʾān itself adduces no sign but the Qurʾān (§15, Q 17:59, 13:7, 29:51) is the wedge he will drive between these two camps. muʿjiza / iʿjāz / taḥaddī are the prophetological anchor terms (glossary §VII).
§12 — Against iʿjāz (1): inimitability would not prove prophethood, since eloquence admits of degrees; and a universal sign must be recognizable by all, not only by the Arabs

As for what they claimed of the inimitability of the Qurʾān (iʿjāz al-Qurʾān), they have been bound by [several] things concerning it. Among them: that even were the matter as they mentioned — that the eloquent ones of the Arabs did not oppose it — it would not follow from that that it is inimitable (muʿjizan), nor would there be in it a proof of prophethood, since people may surpass one another in the knowledge of language, eloquence, and fluency. And if that is so, it is admissible that he was the most eloquent of the folk, the most fluent of them, and the highest of them in rank in this respect, so that they were not strong enough against him in it.

And among that: that if he was sent, as is stated, to all creation — the Arab and the non-Arab — then it ought to have been that he bring a sign and a proof which they would, in their entirety, know to be inimitable. But the Qurʾān — the rest of the foreigners (al-aʿjām) and the rest of the nations and creeds, who do not understand the language of the Arab, do not know it to be inimitable, since they hear only a speech of which they do not know what it is. And likewise also the rest of the Arabs, who do know the language of the Arab, do not know it to be inimitable — just as they hear much poetry and oratory and yet it is not, in their estimation, inimitable — since they are not skilled enough to bring its like. And, on your statement, only a small band stands upon its being inimitable — perhaps ten persons, or fewer, who are the most eloquent of the Arabs and the most knowing of them in speech. So is it admissible that God send a prophet to all creation, and give him for that a proof and an argument which binds only ten of them, to the exclusion of the rest of them?

: Two distinct objections to iʿjāz. (1) Inimitability does not entail miracle: superlative eloquence is a difference of degree within a natural human capacity; that no contemporary out-wrote Muḥammad shows at most that he was the most eloquent Arab, not that the Qurʾān transcends human power. (2) A universal sign must be universally recognizable: a prophet sent to "all creation" (the Arab and the aʿjām, the non-Arabophone nations) must offer a sign all can verify; but only Arabic-literate connoisseurs can even assess the Qurʾān's eloquence — "perhaps ten persons or fewer." A proof accessible to ten cannot ground a mission to all. This second point recurs as Q's leitmotif: the alleged proof is parochial, not universal. al-aʿjām = non-Arabs / non-Arabophones.
§13 — Against iʿjāz (2): the non-opposition is an unproven report; the rival oppositions may have been suppressed; and non-opposition need not stem from inability

And among that: that their saying that the folk did not oppose him is a claim that has not been established, and upon which no proof stands; rather this is [merely] a report concerning him. And what is there to deny that they may have opposed him with numerous oppositions (muʿāraḍāt ʿidād), and then, when the matter was completed for him, the hand was loosed, and the dominion was knit together, those oppositions were hunted down, burnt, and abolished — since they had not [yet] spread nor multiplied — just as the Qurʾān of Musaylima was abolished?

And again: even if it were established that they did not oppose him, it would not be established that that was on account of an inability (ʿajz) on their part — since it is admissible that they reckoned that opposition needs reflection and time, and that, were they to oppose him, he would say to them, "this is not like what I said," and the dispute would multiply, and disagreement would fall out, and the matter would revert to the sword; so that when the matter stood thus, occupying oneself with opposition would be without meaning, since, alongside occupying oneself with it, the [political] management would not hold. So they left that off for this cause.

: Two further objections. (1) The non-opposition is unattested — a bare report, not a demonstrated fact; rival "oppositions" (muʿāraḍāt) may well have been produced and then suppressed once Muḥammad held power, exactly as the rival "Qurʾān" of Musaylima (the rival prophet of the Ridda, d. 11/632) was destroyed. (2) Even granting non-opposition, it need not stem from ʿajz (inability) — it could be prudential: opposition demanded leisure and reflection, invited the retort "this is not like mine," and risked recourse to the sword; abstention may have been political calculation, not literary incapacity. Both objections sever the inference from non-opposition to inimitability.
§14 — Against iʿjāz (3): the challenge itself shows the "proof" is one whose completion depends on the opponents — a "poor" proof

And this is a problem against them. It is said to them: tell us about your man — when he called the Arabs to oppose him, and informed them that their inability for that is his proof of the soundness of his prophethood: does that not indicate that his miracle was completed and made sound only by their act? For else, had they said to him, "you call us to oppose you, and you allege that by our inability your argument is established and your proof stands; but opposition needs time and the ranging of reflection, with a mind at leisure, and we are not energetic for any of this, nor free for it, nor do we wish to occupy ourselves with it. So if you are, as you allege, a prophet, then bring us a proof self-sufficient in itself (burhān ghaniyy bi-nafsihi), in which we are not needed, and in which our inability is not the proof — for this proof which you claim is a poor proof (dalīl faqīr), since it is completed only by another than you" — was that not [an option open] to them? So this is [the predicament] in their claim of the inimitability of the Qurʾān and its [serving as] proof.

: The most elegant of Q's anti-iʿjāz arguments, turning on the structure of the taḥaddī itself. A genuine prophetic sign should be self-sufficient (ghaniyy bi-nafsihi) — evidential in its own right. But the iʿjāz argument makes the proof depend on the opponents' failure: it is established only by their inability. Q dramatizes the Arabs' fair reply — "give us a proof that does not need us" — and brands the iʿjāz a dalīl faqīr, a "poor" (needy, dependent) proof, contrasted with the burhān ghaniyy a true prophet would supply. The faqīr / ghaniyy (poor/rich, i.e. dependent/self-sufficient) wordplay is Q's own coinage for the point.
§15 — Against the reported miracles: the Qurʾān itself disclaims any sign but the Qurʾān, and Muḥammad excuses the absence of signs

As for whoever claimed for him the rest of the miracles which we mentioned some of — it is said to them: how is it admissible that there be for your man a miracle, when he did not mention in his book that he performed [any] miracle, nor turned an eye [from blind to seeing], nor altered anything from its nature? Indeed, together with [the fact] that he mentioned nothing of that and did not claim it, he even disavows that and excuses himself from it in more than one place of his book. Of that is his saying [דקראן = al-Qurʾān 17:59] "wa-mā manaʿanā an nursila bi-l-āyāti illā an kadhdhaba bihā l-awwalūn" ("and nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them") — for is this not an explicit declaration that he brought no sign? And of that is his saying [Q 13:7] "wa-idhā yasʾalūnaka ʿani l-āyāti fa-qul al-āyātu ʿinda llāhi" ("and when they ask you about the signs, say: the signs are with God"), and his saying also [Q 13:7] "innamā anta nadhīrun wa-li-kulli qawmin hādin" ("you are but a warner, and for every people there is a guide"). [So] let him stand aside, who claims a miracle for this man, [in the face of] these sayings.

: Against the supplementary muʿjizāt (§11): the Qurʾān itself disclaims any sign but the Qurʾān, and even apologizes for the absence of signs. Q quotes Q 17:59 ("nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them" — a verse traditionally read as explaining why Muḥammad worked no signs), Q 13:7 ("the signs are with God"; "you are only a warner"). If the Qurʾān concedes Muḥammad performed no signs, the later miracle-traditions (tree, water, speaking ewe) are post hoc inventions contradicting scripture. §16 — Against the mass-transmission (tawātur) of the miracles: the chains thin out to a tiny original few; the miracle-reports occur only in the maghāzī, and the Qurʾān's own a-wa-lam yakfihim disclaims them

So if they make a plea by the transmission of the widely-attested reports (naql al-akhbār al-mutawātira) and the multitude of the transmitters, of whose like collusion (al-tawāṭuʾ) is inadmissible — it is said to them: the argument is not in the multitude of the transmitters, but rather the argument is in the multitude of those from whom it is transmitted — those who witnessed [the event] and [from whom] he [the original eyewitness] performed [the report]. For you, even if your transmitters in these witnessed [recent] epochs have [indeed] mentioned what you claim, [yet] whenever it is carried back to an earlier generation (khalf), it dwindles and diminishes, until the root [of the chain] comes to rest upon a scant group and a few persons — and they are the ten of whom that was related. And a company of you allege that the report of the miracles is not found

: The anti-tawātur argument: mass-transmission (tawātur) guarantees truth only if the originating witnesses are many; a chain of millions today is worthless if it funnels back to a handful of original reporters. Q claims the miracle-reports do precisely this — thinning out (tankharit wa-taqill) as one ascends the isnād until the source is "the ten" (a recurring figure in the bab for the tiny qualified few). The decisive naql-vs.-manqūl-ʿanhum distinction (witnesses from whom it is transmitted vs. later transmitters) is the kalām commonplace on the conditions of valid tawātur. Note the structural mirror to the iʿjāz argument: there only ten could judge the eloquence; here only ten originate the miracle-reports.

except in the campaign-narratives (al-maghāzī), and that the maghāzī were related by none but Muḥammad b. Isḥāq — and this is what we have heard from a number of them. And our sufficiency [in the matter] is the saying of your man [דין = al-Qurʾān 29:51] "a-wa-lam yakfihim annā anzalnā ʿalayka l-Qurʾān" ("does it not suffice them that We have sent down upon you the Qurʾān?") — for, had there been there a miracle other than it, would he not have added to this statement, saying, "and how [should they doubt], when We have brought such-and-such, and done such-and-such"? So this is what the place can bear of the mention of what [tells] against them.

And I have exhausted that, bab by bab, in the book which I composed against them, and I mentioned in it also questions that passed between me and a group of their mutakallimūn; so whoever inspects it will stand upon the weakness of their case and its frailty, and his certitude in the God of Israel and in His law, which is His Torah, will increase.

: Q's source-critical coup: the miracle-reports are confined to the maghāzī (the campaign/biography literature, the sīra), and these go back to a single transmitter, Muḥammad b. Isḥāq (Ibn Isḥāq, d. ~150/767, author of the Sīra) — so the supposed tawātur collapses to a single originating authority, the antithesis of mass-transmission. This is a strikingly precise piece of Muslim source-criticism from a 10th-century Karaite, naming the Sīra's author and isolating him as the lone channel. (The OCR confirms the name محمد بن إسحق in the bab16 file, p198.) : Q clinches with Q 29:51 (a-wa-lam yakfihim annā anzalnā ʿalayka l-Kitāb/al-Qurʾān) — "does it not suffice them that We sent down the Qurʾān?": had Muḥammad worked other signs, the Qurʾān would have adduced them here rather than resting on itself, so the verse is itself evidence that the Qurʾān was his only claimed sign. The bab closes with the second reference to Q's lost dedicated anti-Muslim kitāb (see n. 1), in which he reports having debated Muslim mutakallimūn in person — a valuable notice of Q's live Baghdad disputation activity. The heading — partly OCR-corrupted but recoverable (the name מִחַמַּדּ = Muḥammad survives, against the Kraken "ימול," diff-report p207 rows 3–4) — is fī al-radd ʿalā al-Muslimīn wa-ʿalā kull man athbata nubuwwat Muḥammad: "the refutation of the Muslims and of everyone who has affirmed the prophethood of Muḥammad." - Two-part architecture. The bab falls cleanly into two movements. (I) §§1–11a: the Torah's law is not abrogated and no later prophet was foretold — built on (a) self-contradiction (Muḥammad affirms the Torah he abrogates), (b) the naṣṣ of perpetuity (Num 15:23, Exod 31:16, Lev 23:21), (c) the seal of prophecy in Malachi and Daniel, (d) the silence-of-the-prophets reductio, (e) the tawātur argument that the transmission of non-abrogation is as sound as the transmission of the Torah itself, and (f) the logic-of-repentance argument (restoration to the law presupposes the law stands). (II) §§11b–16: the proofs of Muḥammad's prophethood fail — the iʿjāz al-Qurʾān (four objections, §§12–14) and the reported muʿjizāt (§§15–16), capped by source-criticism of the maghāzī.

- Prophetology vocabulary (glossary §VII). This bab is the first to instantiate the staged §VII anchor terms. al-nubuwwa (prophethood) is the contested predicate throughout. al-muʿjiza / al-muʿjizāt (the [evidentiary] miracle[s]) is rendered "miracle," with the technical sense = an act establishing prophethood by transcending human power; iʿjāz al-Qurʾān = "the inimitability of the Qurʾān," the doctrine that the Qurʾān's own muʿjiza-status lies in its unsurpassable eloquence. al-taḥaddī = "the challenge" (to produce its like). The fourth staged term, al-ifḥām (reducing the opponent to silence), does not surface lexically in this bab, though Q enacts it in the Yashūʿ-Paddā debate of Bab 16 §16; it should be carried forward to §VII when Bab 16 is glossed. Two Q-coinages deserve glossary entry: dalīl faqīr ("a poor/needy proof") vs. burhān ghaniyy bi-nafsihi ("a self-sufficient proof") — the §14 contrast that is the rhetorical core of the anti-iʿjāz polemic.
